services.body:
## Solvent cleans oil. It does not clean sweat.

Dry cleaning is a wash in solvent rather than water. We run a solvent that is gentler on fibre and finish than the older perc systems still common in Gurugram. Solvent is very good at what water struggles with: body oil, the sebum ring inside a collar, ghee and cooking grease, make-up, car grime. It is close to useless on water-based staining — perspiration, tea, coffee, cold drink, juice, wine, most gravies. Those have to be lifted by hand first, on a spotting board with steam, vacuum and the correct agent for that stain group, before the garment goes anywhere near a machine.

This is where dry cleaning is actually won or lost. A shop that skips pre-spotting hands back a garment that smells clean with the mark still sitting in it. It is also why we ask what the spill was. Tannin, protein, oil and dye each need a different treatment, and the wrong one can set a stain permanently instead of removing it. One of our customers put it plainly: "I tried at home and the stain didn't go. Wash4You removed it completely." Nothing clever happened there — we just identified the stain before treating it.

## Every piece is inspected before it is processed

Fibre first, care label second. Sarees, lehengas and sherwanis very often arrive with no label at all, or with a tailor's label that says nothing useful, so the fabric has to be identified by hand and eye. We then test for colour bleed on an inside seam or hem — non-negotiable for bandhani, leheriya, hand-dyed cotton, and for anything with a dark border sitting against a pale body, like a maroon-bordered cream Kanjeevaram.

Embellishment decides the method. Zari and dabka can tarnish, plastic sequins can soften in solvent or under a press, and mukaish and stone-work is often glued rather than stitched. Heavily worked pieces are covered, tacked with muslin, or cleaned by hand and spot-treated only — never tumbled. Nazuk kapde, extra care: that means slower work, not a different marketing word. Beads and stones are counted at intake and checked again at packing, and any existing damage is noted on your receipt before the garment leaves your door.

## What we cannot save — and will tell you upfront

Chlorine damage is permanent. Splash from a toilet or bathroom cleaner, hair bleach, or benzoyl peroxide acne cream on a collar or pillowcase destroys the dye itself; there is nothing left to clean. Sugar stains from juice or cold drink go in invisible and oxidise into brown caramel over months in storage — once they have browned, they are usually there for good. Heat sets stains, so a mark that has already been ironed over is far harder. Mehendi and permanent marker are dyes and behave like dyes. And a garment already weakened at the underarm by years of antiperspirant and sweat can split during finishing — the damage was there before it reached us, but you deserve to hear it in advance rather than at delivery.

## What we clean in, and why it matters

Not all dry cleaning is the same chemical. The industry standard for fifty years was perchloroethylene — perc — and a lot of shops in Gurugram still run it. We use a different solvent instead.

Our solvent is a refined petroleum distillate, purified to strip the aromatics and impurities you would find in fuel. It is not a "green" solvent and we will not pretend otherwise. What it is, is a much gentler one. It dissolves body oil, collar sebum, ghee and cooking grease, make-up and traffic grime, without the aggression that makes perc hard on dyes, sequins, beadwork and finishes over repeated cleans.

That gentleness has a cost, and it is ours to carry rather than yours: a cycle with our solvent runs longer than a perc cycle to reach the same result, and on very heavy grease perc is still the more brutal tool. We would rather run the slower machine and keep your lehenga's zari intact.

The solvent runs in a closed loop. It is filtered and distilled after every load and returned to the tank, so the same solvent is recovered and reused rather than discharged.

**What you actually notice**

- Nothing smells of chemicals when it comes back. Perc leaves a characteristic sharp odour; our solvent does not.
- Colours hold. Dyes, prints and metallic finishes survive repeat cleaning far better.
- Delicates come back the same size. Less shrinkage and less fibre stress on silk, wool and pashmina.
- Perc is classified as a probable human carcinogen. Our solvent is not — which matters most for the people who work with it every day, and for anything that sits in your wardrobe afterwards.

## Before you hand it over

Empty every pocket, especially of tissues. Remove brooches and detachable buttons. Tell us about spills you can no longer see — a clear one today is a brown one in six months. And tell us honestly if you have already tried something at home, because nail-polish remover, hot water or a supermarket stain remover changes what we can safely do next.

what_we_clean.detail: Jacket and trousers are cleaned together as a set even when only one half looks dirty, so the two never drift apart in shade. Finished over a form with steam and vacuum rather than pressed flat, which is what prevents shine on worsted wool and bubbling over fused interlining.
Colour-fastness tested at an inside hem before anything else, since a dark border against a pale body is the most common bleed risk. Pleats and pallu are set by hand at finishing.

The base net, the can-can lining and the embroidered panels all react differently, which is what causes puckering when a heavy ghagra is cleaned carelessly. Worked sections are hand-treated and the skirt is re-set rather than flattened.
Structured chest canvas and collar stiffening need controlled heat. Zari buttons and thread-work are protected before cleaning and hand-finished after.
Dry cleaning also clears moth larvae, which is exactly why woollens should go into storage clean — moths feed on food, sweat and body-oil residue, not on the wool itself.
Sequins, beadwork, mukaish, stone-work and appliqué. Assessed piece by piece; some items are spot-cleaned by hand only, and we will say so before we accept the order.
Linings, boning and pleating are checked separately from the outer shell. Velvet is steamed from the reverse, never pressed face-down.
Collar and cuff grime is pre-treated by hand before the main clean, since that soiling is oil-based and concentrated where the fabric meets skin.

process.detail: Every piece is counted and logged with you before it leaves, and you get a written receipt of exactly what was collected. Your order is bagged on its own and never shares a load with anyone else's.
Fibre identified, care label read where one exists, existing damage recorded, and embellishments counted. Anything we think may not survive cleaning is flagged to you at this stage, not after.

Steam and form-pressing rather than flat pressing where the garment is structured. Embroidery, zari and pleating are finished by hand.
Re-inspected against the intake notes, embellishments re-counted, then returned on hangers under a breathable cover to your door.

faqs.q: Should I dry clean my lehenga straight after the function, or can it wait?
faqs.a: Send it as soon as you can. The stains you cannot see are the problem — sweat, perfume, juice and cold drink go in clear and oxidise into brown patches over the months a wedding outfit sits in a cupboard. By the time you notice them at the next wedding, they are often permanent. The same applies to woollens going into storage.

faqs.q: My saree has zari and sequins. Is it safe to dry clean?
faqs.a: It depends on the work, which is why we inspect before quoting a method. Metallic zari can tarnish, plastic sequins can soften in solvent or under heat, and stone-work is frequently glued rather than stitched. Pieces like these are covered or tacked and cleaned by hand and spot-treated, not tumbled. If we do not think an item will come through safely, we will tell you at the counter.

faqs.q: Can you remove haldi or turmeric stains?
faqs.a: Often we can lighten them a great deal, sometimes completely, but turmeric is a genuine natural dye and we will not promise it. It also reacts to alkaline treatment by shifting from yellow towards red, so a home remedy applied first can make our job harder. Bring it in untouched and unironed if possible.

faqs.q: Only my suit trousers are dirty. Can I send just those?
faqs.a: You can, but we would rather you did not. Trousers are worn far more often than the jacket, and cleaning them separately over a few years leaves the two halves at visibly different shades. Send the suit as a set and it stays a suit.

faqs.q: What happens if the stain doesn't come out?
faqs.a: We tell you what it is and why. Some things genuinely cannot be reversed — chlorine bleach damage, caramelised sugar stains, mehendi, and marks that have already been heat-set by ironing. We would rather return an honest answer than repeat an aggressive treatment that thins the fabric or lifts the colour around the mark.

faqs.q: I already tried removing the stain at home. Does that matter?
faqs.a: Yes, very much, so please tell us. Nail-polish remover, hot water, chlorine bleach and supermarket stain removers all change the chemistry of what is left behind, and one of them can rule out the treatment we would otherwise have used. It is not a problem to admit — it just changes our approach.

faqs.a: Pickup and delivery are free across Gurugram. Message or call +91 63 67 600 500 to book a slot; your items are counted with you at the door and you get a signed acknowledgement of exactly what was collected. You can also drop items at our Vyapar Kendra store in Sushant Lok Phase I, Sector 43, or at Unitech Arcadia in Sector 49.

faqs.q: Do you handle woollens and pashmina shawls?
faqs.a: Yes. Dry cleaning is the right method for wool and pashmina, and it has the added benefit of clearing moth larvae. Store them clean and out of polythene afterwards — sealed plastic traps moisture and yellows both wool and silk over time.

faqs.q: What solvent do you use for dry cleaning, and how is it different?
faqs.a: Dry cleaning is a wash in solvent instead of water, and the solvent is the difference. Most shops use perchloroethylene — perc — which cleans hard but is aggressive on dyes, embellishment and delicate fibre, and is classified as a probable human carcinogen. We use a different solvent, a refined petroleum distillate that is gentler on fabric and finish and far less toxic. It runs a longer cycle to get the same result, which is a trade we are happy to make on a saree or a suit.

faqs.q: Is your dry-cleaning solvent eco-friendly?
faqs.a: It is much better than perc, but we would not call it green and you should be sceptical of anyone who does. Our solvent is petroleum-derived. What is true: it is not a classified carcinogen, it emits far fewer volatile compounds, it is not a groundwater contaminant the way perc is, and our machine runs a closed loop that filters and distils the solvent after every load so it is reused rather than discharged. For genuinely water-safe items we use wet cleaning instead, which is the greener option where the fabric allows it.

## Sorting is most of the job

Almost everything that goes wrong in a wash is decided before the machine starts. We sort your order three ways: by colour, by fabric weight, and by how soiled it is. Colour matters most on anything new. Unwashed dark denim, maroon and deep red cotton, and cheap black tees shed loose dye for the first three or four washes, and once that dye has been through heat it is fixed for good. Tell us if a piece has never been washed and it goes in separately. Fabric weight matters because a bath towel tumbling against a fine cotton shirt will abrade the shirt. Soil level matters because kitchen clothes and gym wear need a longer main wash than a shirt worn for four hours in an air-conditioned office.

## Gurugram water, and why whites go grey

Much of Gurugram runs on hard groundwater. Calcium and magnesium react with detergent and leave a film that builds up wash after wash: whites turn a dull grey, towels stiffen and stop absorbing, dark cottons pick up a chalky cast. Adding more detergent makes it worse, because the undissolved detergent is the residue. We dose to the load and the water and run an extra rinse rather than a bigger scoop. If your whites have already greyed over years of home washing we can lift them noticeably, but we cannot return them to day-one white, and anyone promising that is selling optical brightener, which washes straight back out.

## What we cannot save

Underarm yellowing on white shirts is aluminium from antiperspirant bonded into the fibre along with body protein. We reduce it; we do not erase it. Bleach marks from toilet cleaner or hair dye splash are missing colour rather than added dirt, and nothing cleans colour back in. A stain that has already been ironed or tumble-dried is usually permanent, because heat sets oil and protein alike. Most common of all: a stain scrubbed hard at home with bar soap and a brush leaves a fuzzy, faded patch where the fibre has broken, and that damage is done before we ever see the garment. So leave the stain alone and tell us what caused it. The treatment for oil is the opposite of the treatment for blood, milk or egg, and hot water on a protein stain sets it permanently.

## Before you hand the bag over

Empty every pocket. One ballpoint pen can mark a whole load and one tissue will coat it in lint. Close zips and fasten hooks so they do not snag knitwear. Count your own socks, hankies and innerwear, since small items are what people notice missing. Keep out anything embellished: sequins, mirror work, beaded kurtas, silk, wool and suits belong in dry cleaning, not in a wash-and-fold load.

## What comes back

Your order is counted with you at the door, written on a receipt you keep, bagged on its own and washed as its own load. It never shares a drum with another household's clothes. It comes back dried at a controlled temperature, folded and packed. Wash and fold means clean and neatly folded, not pressed. If you want crisp collars and sharp trousers, ask for wash with steam ironing instead. One last thing: don't leave the sealed pack in a damp cupboard through the monsoon. Open it and let the clothes breathe.

what_we_clean.detail: Cotton, linen and cotton blends worn for work or at home. Collars and cuffs get a separate pre-treat before the main wash, because that is where body oil and Gurugram dust collect first.
Denim is washed inside out and cool to slow fading. New dark jeans go in on their own for the first few washes so the indigo does not travel.

Synthetic performance fabric holds odour in the fibre rather than on it. It needs a cool wash and a proper rinse; hot water and heavy softener are what make gym clothes smell again the moment you sweat.
Frequent, gentle washing rather than aggressive chemistry, so name tapes, printed logos and elastic survive the term.

faqs.q: Do you take laundry for a short stay or a few weeks only?

If someone in the house has eczema or reacts to fragrance, say so when you book and we will keep the order fragrance-free.

## A shoe is not one thing

Take a running shoe apart in your head. Knit or mesh upper, suede or synthetic overlays, a foam midsole, a rubber outsole, a printed logo, a fabric-backed insole, and glue holding most of it together. Six materials, six different reactions to water, heat and detergent. A washing machine treats all six identically, which is exactly why shoes come out of one looking worse than they went in. Everything we do at Wash4You is by hand, panel by panel, at the two stores in Sushant Lok Phase I and Unitech Arcadia.

In Gurugram the soiling is fairly predictable. Fine construction dust that works into mesh and seams; iron-rich reddish soil from the Aravalli side that stains light foam; monsoon mud that dries into the outsole tread; rubber crumb from the turf grounds; and gym and office shoes where the real problem is the insole, not the upper.

## Suede, and why water marks are not dirt

Most "stained" suede we see is a tide line, not a stain. Someone spot-cleaned one patch, the wet area dried at a different rate from the dry area, and the boundary set as a permanent-looking ring. The fix is counter-intuitive: instead of attacking the mark, we take the whole panel to an even level of wetness, work it with a brass and rubber brush along the nap, then dry it slowly in shade with the shoe supported so it holds its shape. The nap is re-raised at the end. That is how the Nike SB Dunk in our before/after came back — no bleaching, no re-dyeing, the original suede simply made even again.

## Soles, whitening and an honest limit

White midsoles and gum soles yellow for two reasons. One is ordinary UV oxidation of the rubber over years. The other — much more common — is a home wash where alkaline detergent was not fully rinsed out and the shoe was then dried in direct Gurugram sun. The second is largely reversible: neutralise the residue, dry properly in shade. The first is not. Deep oxidation on an old gum sole can be lightened, and we will lighten it, but returning it to factory colour needs peroxide strong enough to degrade the rubber itself. We would rather hand you a slightly honey-toned sole than a crumbling white one.

## What we will tell you we cannot fix

Oil and grease that has soaked deep into open suede or nubuck. Dye transfer, where colour from a dark sock, a wet dark panel or a car mat has migrated into pale material — that is a dye, not soil. Old polyurethane midsoles that have hydrolysed and crumble under a thumbnail. Shoes already coated in whitener paste, where the coating hides the damage rather than fixing it. Cracked topcoat on creased white leather: the dirt was filling the cracks, so a properly clean shoe can look more creased than a dirty one. Grass staining on foam improves a lot, as the Hoka Bondi shows, but a faint shadow sometimes stays.

We inspect and tell you the honest ceiling before we start. Purane sneakers ko nayi jaan — new life for old sneakers — is realistic surprisingly often. Pretending everything is recoverable is not.

faqs.q: Will you wash my sneakers in a machine?
faqs.a: No. Everything is hand-cleaned, panel by panel, with brushes and solutions chosen for each material. A drum wash flexes the glue lines, distorts knit uppers and packs grit into the foam. It is the single most common reason a shoe arrives at our counter already damaged.

faqs.q: Can you actually clean suede, or will it be ruined?
faqs.a: Suede is our most requested material and the one we are most careful with. It is cleaned with a controlled amount of moisture across a whole panel at a time so it dries evenly, then brushed to raise the nap again. What we cannot reverse is oil or grease that has already soaked into the fibres, and we will tell you that at inspection rather than after.

faqs.q: My white midsoles have gone yellow. Can you make them white again?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. Yellowing from detergent residue and sun-drying after a home wash usually comes back well. Yellowing from years of UV oxidation in the rubber only lightens — full reversal needs chemicals that weaken the sole, and we do not use them. We will show you which one you have.

faqs.q: Do you handle the smell as well as the dirt?
faqs.a: Yes, and the smell almost never lives in the upper. It lives in the insole and the footbed foam, where it is bacterial. Removable insoles are cleaned and dried separately; fixed footbeds get an antibacterial treatment and a proper slow dry. A shoe that is rushed to dry will smell again within a week.

faqs.q: What should I check before handing my shoes over?
faqs.a: Take out custom orthotics or medical insoles and keep them. Tell us about anything you already tried at home, especially bleach, hydrogen peroxide or whitener paste, because it changes what we can safely use. Point out any sole separation or loose stitching so we both note it beforehand. And mention it if the shoe has been painted, re-dyed or customised — those finishes can lift.

faqs.q: Do you clean formal leather shoes and boots too, not just sneakers?
faqs.a: Yes. Leather dress shoes, boots, loafers and sandals are cleaned and conditioned rather than washed, so the leather is not stripped of its oils and left to crack. Football and turf boots, kids' school shoes and canvas shoes are all handled as well.

faqs.q: Do I have to come to the store?
faqs.a: No. Pickup and delivery is free anywhere we serve in Gurugram. Your shoes are counted with you at the door, packed separately from every other customer's order, and you get a written receipt of exactly what was collected. You can also drop them at the Sushant Lok Phase I or Sector 49 store if you prefer.

services.body:
## Why a sofa goes grey before it ever gets stained

Most sofas we are called to in Gurugram have no obvious stain on them. They have simply gone grey along the arms, the headrest line and the front edge of the seat cushions. That is hair oil, body oil and skin contact oxidising over a couple of years, holding on to the fine dust that gets in through balcony doors and lift lobbies. It builds up so gradually that families stop seeing it, then notice it the day a new cushion cover arrives and looks wrong against the sofa. The three-seater in our before-and-after photos was exactly this: no spill, no accident, just years of contact soil, cleaned in the customer's own living room.

## The process, described honestly

Dry soil comes out first. We vacuum the deck, the crevices and the area under the cushions before any liquid touches the fabric. This part is not optional. Water on dry particulate soil turns it into mud at the base of the fibre and pushes it deeper, which is why a wet home cleaning often looks worse a week later.

Next we identify the fabric and test it. A hidden patch, usually the back panel or the underside of a cushion, gets a colour-fastness test before anything else happens. Dark blues, reds and handloom weaves bleed more often than people expect, and a bleeding dye discovered on the back panel is a very different conversation from one discovered on the seat.

The clean itself is a pre-spray, a dwell time, gentle agitation with a soft brush so the solution travels through the pile instead of sitting on top of it, then hot water extraction with an upholstery tool that pulls the soil and the solution back out in the same pass. The real skill is moisture control. Foam that gets saturated stays damp for days, starts to smell, and lets tannins from the wooden frame or jute backing wick upward as it dries. That shows up as brown rings a full day after everything looked perfect. We use the least water that will do the job, then take repeated dry passes and set airflow across the cushions.

## What we cannot save, and will say before we start

Sun-faded panels. The window-side arm on a Gurugram flat takes years of hard light, and once UV has broken the dye there is nothing to clean back. Cleaning the rest can even make that fade more obvious. Deep pet urine that has soaked into the foam: surface treatment helps the smell, but the foam or the cover needs replacing. Denim dye transfer on cream and beige fabric, which is a dye now, not a stain. Turmeric and old oxidised food marks on pale upholstery, where purana daag usually lightens but rarely vanishes. Ballpoint ink on microfibre, where solvent can spread the mark into a halo larger than the original. And rexine or faux leather that has already begun to flake, where cleaning accelerates the peeling. We would rather decline that job than hand it back worse.

## Before we arrive

Clear about a metre around the sofa and take off throws and loose covers. Tell us about anything already applied at home, because a supermarket shampoo or a fabric protector leaves residue that changes how we treat the fabric. Check the seams and piping yourself and point out anything loose, since suction on weak stitching will open it. We need a power socket and access to water. Loose covers and cushion covers can go to the workshop instead, with our free doorstep pickup and delivery.

faqs.q: Do you clean the sofa at our home, or take it away?
faqs.a: At your home. Fixed upholstery is shampooed and extracted in place, in your living room, so nothing has to be dismantled or carried down. Loose covers, cushion covers and small removable items are the exception: those can go to the workshop and come back on our free pickup and delivery.

faqs.q: How long before we can sit on it again?
faqs.a: It depends on the fabric, how dense the foam is and how much airflow the room gets, so we will not quote you a fixed number. We will tell you what to expect for your sofa before we start, and we stand cushions on edge and set airflow before we leave. As a rule, the less water a job needs, the sooner you are back on it.

faqs.q: Will the colour run or fade?
faqs.a: We test a hidden area for colour-fastness before anything else happens, usually the back panel or under a cushion. Dark blues, reds and handloom weaves are the usual risks. If a fabric bleeds, we will show you the test swab and switch to a low-moisture method or advise against cleaning altogether rather than take a chance with your sofa.

faqs.q: Can you get rid of a pet smell?
faqs.a: Partly, and it depends how deep it went. Urine sitting on the surface of the fabric responds well. Urine that has soaked through the cover into the foam is a different problem, because the source is inside the cushion where no surface treatment reaches. In that case honest advice is to replace the foam or the cover. We will tell you which situation you are in once we have inspected it.

faqs.q: Do you clean leather and rexine sofas the same way?
faqs.a: No. Leather is never extraction cleaned. It is cleaned and conditioned by hand with pH-balanced products, which is our separate leather care service. Rexine and faux leather can be surface cleaned, but if the coating has started to flake or peel we will tell you that cleaning will speed that up, and we would rather not do it.

faqs.q: What do you need from us on the day?
faqs.a: A power socket near the sofa, access to water, and roughly a metre of clear space around the piece so the tool can reach every panel. Please mention beforehand if any home shampoo, stain spray or fabric protector has been used, and point out torn seams or loose piping before we begin.

## The dry soil comes out before any water goes in

A rug that has spent two years on a Gurugram floor is holding more dry grit than most people expect — NCR road dust, construction fines from the tower next door, and whatever the balcony door lets in through the winter. That grit sits at the base of the pile, below the level you can see or feel, and it is abrasive. Every footstep grinds it against the wool and shortens the life of the rug.

It also has to leave before anything wet arrives, because water turns dry soil into mud and drives it into the foundation. So the first stage of a proper rug wash is purely mechanical: the rug is dusted from the reverse, repeatedly, until nothing more falls out. This is the single biggest difference between a rug that is washed and a rug that has been shampooed where it lay. The shampoo-only job looks good for a fortnight and then goes flat.

## Fibre identification decides the method, not the price

Wool, silk, cotton, jute and polypropylene all behave differently in water, so we identify the fibre before we commit to a method. The one to be careful about is viscose — sold as art silk, banana silk or faux silk, and very common in rugs bought off a showroom floor. Viscose is regenerated cellulose. It loses a large part of its strength when wet, the pile can dry stiff and yellowed, and once it browns the colour is inside the fibre rather than on it. If your rug is viscose we will tell you the realistic outcome before we take it, not after.

## Dye stability

Hand-knotted Persian, Kashmiri and Indian pieces often carry reds and indigos that were never fully fixed. Every colour is tested with a damp white cloth before washing, and unstable dyes are held with an acidic rinse. Bleeding that has already happened in an earlier wash — the pink halo around a red medallion — can sometimes be reduced. It cannot always be removed.

## What cannot be brought back

Bleach spots and sun fade are dye loss, not soil. No cleaning process puts colour back into a fibre; that is a re-dyeing job for a weaver. Pile crush in the traffic lane of a machine-made polypropylene rug is heat-set fibre — the colour will lift, the pile height will not. Moth damage: washing kills larvae and removes the keratin they feed on, but bare patches stay bare.

And on wool, be realistic about spills that are themselves dyes. Wool is a protein fibre and accepts acid dyes readily, which is exactly what children's fruit drinks, food colouring, Holi colour and some red wines are. They bond the way dye is meant to. We usually improve them substantially. We do not promise to erase them.

## Pet urine is chemistry, not a stain

The odour lives in the foundation and backing, not in the pile, which is why topical sprays only postpone it. It has to be flushed and rinsed right through. Urine is also alkaline enough to strip dye out of wool permanently — that yellow or orange patch left behind is dye damage, and cleaning will not reverse it.

## Drying is where rugs are actually ruined

Wool held damp in Gurugram monsoon humidity develops odour and cellulosic browning within a day. Cotton foundations shrink unevenly when one end dries faster than the other, and the rug comes back wavy and out of square. Controlled, even, fast drying matters more than the wash itself.

faqs.q: How do I know whether my rug is real silk or viscose?
faqs.a: Real silk is a protein fibre and viscose is cellulose, so they behave differently in water — which matters a great deal before washing. Two rough home checks: viscose feels cool and slightly slippery and its pile often looks unnaturally shiny in one direction only, and a viscose rug will usually feel much heavier than a silk rug of the same size. We test a stray fibre from the underside or fringe before we commit to a method, and we will show you what we found. If it turns out to be viscose, we will explain what a realistic result looks like before starting.

faqs.q: Can you remove pet urine odour completely?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if it is flushed and rinsed rather than sprayed. The odour lives in the foundation and backing, so topical treatment only masks it for a few weeks. What we cannot reverse is the dye damage — urine is alkaline enough to pull colour out of wool permanently, and the yellow or orange patch left behind is a re-dyeing job, not a cleaning one. If there are old spots you already know about, point them out at pickup so we can look at them before we quote.

faqs.q: Will the colours run?
faqs.a: That is the exact question we ask before touching the rug. Every colour is tested with a damp white cloth first, and unstable dyes are held with an acidic rinse during washing. Older hand-knotted Persian, Kashmiri and Indian pieces are the ones most likely to have unfixed reds and indigos. If a rug has already bled in a previous wash, we can often reduce the halo, but we will tell you honestly whether it will fully clear.

faqs.q: Do you clean fitted wall-to-wall carpet at home, or does it have to come to you?
faqs.a: Fitted carpet is cleaned in your home — it cannot come off the floor. Loose rugs are collected and washed properly off site, which is the only way to do the dusting and rinsing stages that fitted carpet cannot receive. We handle both, and we take the rug away and bring it back ourselves as part of free pickup and delivery across Gurugram.

faqs.q: My carpet looked clean, then a stain reappeared two days later. Why?
faqs.a: That is wicking, and it means the previous cleaning put in more water than it took out. The stain was never only on the surface — it had soaked down into the backing and the underlay. As the carpet dries, moisture travels upward and carries the residue back to the tips of the pile. The fix is thorough extraction and controlled drying rather than more cleaning solution. If this has happened to your carpet before, tell us, because it changes how we approach it.

faqs.q: Can washing get rid of carpet moths?
faqs.a: Washing kills larvae and eggs and removes the soiling and keratin they feed on, which breaks the cycle. What it cannot do is regrow the pile they have already eaten — bare or thin patches need a weaver, not a cleaner. Check the underside and the areas under furniture, because moth damage almost always starts in the parts of the rug nobody walks on or sees.

faqs.q: What should I check before handing my rug over?
faqs.a: Walk the rug with our team at pickup and look for four things: loose or unravelling fringe, curling or split edges, existing pale patches under furniture, and any earlier repairs. Photograph anything you are unsure about. Every item is counted with you at the door and you get a written receipt of exactly what was collected, so the condition noted at pickup is on record for both sides.

## Dry soil first, water later

The most important step happens before anything gets wet. A curtain that has hung for a year in Gurugram holds a surprising amount of dry soil: construction dust from the tower next door, road grit, and in kitchen-facing rooms a fine oily film that the dust sticks to. Put that straight into water and the dust turns to mud and drives deeper into the weave instead of lifting out. So every panel is dry-soil cleared first: heaviest at the header, and along the bottom 20 cm, always the dirtiest part of a floor-length curtain.

If your curtains look faintly striped once they are down, that is not fading. Dust only lands on the outward face of each pleat, so a pleated panel soils in vertical bands. It comes out.

## What actually decides the method

The care label matters less than what is inside the panel. We check three things at your window: whether the lining is detachable or sewn in, whether there is an interlining (the soft bump layer inside heavy drapes), and what kind of blackout you have. Coated three-pass blackout and a separate blackout lining behave nothing alike in water. Interlined drapes we do not wet clean at all, because the inner layer shifts and bunches inside the panel and there is no getting it flat again.

Cotton and linen shrink. Lined cotton shrinks unevenly, because face fabric and lining move at different rates, and you end up with a rippled hem and a drop that is suddenly short of the floor. That is why a lot of curtain work is dry cleaned rather than washed, even when the label says washable.

## What cannot be saved

Better you know before we take them down.

- **Sun rot.** UV degrades the fibre itself, worst on the leading vertical edge and the top few inches. The cloth looks fine, then tears like wet paper. Nothing reverses it, and cleaning is usually what exposes it, so we pinch-test suspect panels with you standing there.
- **Perished blackout coating.** Once the rubberised backing has gone tacky or chalky with age and heat, it sheds during cleaning. It cannot be re-coated.
- **Old mildew spotting** on linings, from monsoon damp or condensation near a split AC. The mould has stained the fibre, and bleaching it out would take the cloth with it.
- **Heat-set yellowing on polyester sheers.** Optical whiteners work on cotton. They do very little for oxidised polyester.

## Before we arrive

Clear the sill and the pelmet, and tell us if any rod or bracket feels loose. Plastic wall plugs in drywall let go easily, and our terms exclude fixtures that were already weak. We would far rather flag it than discover it.

One thing people regret skipping: poore room ke parde ek saath, clean every panel in a room and not only the marked one. A freshly cleaned panel hanging beside one that was left will not match, and you cannot unsee it.

Hooks, rings and hem weights come off, counted and logged with you at the door like any other order, on a written receipt. On rehang we dress the pleats by hand and tie them loosely so the folds set.

faqs.q: Do I have to take the curtains down myself?
faqs.a: No. Removal and reinstallation are included free with curtain cleaning. Our team brings a ladder, takes the panels off the rod, removes the hooks and rings, and puts everything back and dresses the pleats when the curtains return. You do not need to do anything except clear the sill and point us at the windows.

faqs.q: How long will my windows be bare?
faqs.a: Curtain cleaning takes longer than garment work because of the drying and pressing involved, and heavy lined drapes take the longest. We will give you the expected return date at pickup, before anything leaves the house, so you can plan around it. If you have a bedroom you cannot leave uncovered, tell us and we can schedule that room separately from the rest.

faqs.q: Will my curtains shrink?
faqs.a: Cotton, linen and unlined cotton-blend curtains carry a real risk, especially if they have never been cleaned since they were stitched. Lined panels are the trickier case, because the face fabric and the lining shrink at different rates and the hem ripples. Where that risk is present we will normally recommend dry cleaning instead of washing, even if the care label says the fabric is washable, and we will tell you at pickup rather than after.

faqs.q: Can you steam-clean the curtains on the rod without taking them down?
faqs.a: Steaming in place freshens the look and relaxes creases, but it does not remove embedded dust from inside the weave, and it does nothing for the lining, which is usually the dirtier layer. We would rather not sell it as a substitute for a proper clean. If the panels are genuinely only a season old, it can buy you time.

faqs.q: One of my rods is loose. Will you fix it?
faqs.a: We are cleaners, not carpenters, so we will not re-drill or replug a fixture. What we will do is check the rods and brackets before we touch them and tell you if something is unsafe. Our published curtain cleaning policy is explicit that weak or already-damaged rods, brackets and fixtures are not our responsibility, which is exactly why we flag them first rather than pulling and hoping.

faqs.q: My curtains looked darker before. Did cleaning fade them?
faqs.a: Almost always no. Dust settles evenly across a hanging panel and masks fading that has already happened underneath it, so the colour looks deeper than it really is. Take the dust away and you see the true, sun-lightened fabric for the first time. It is one of the most common misunderstandings in this job, which is why we point out visible fading at the window before we take anything down.

faqs.q: What happens if something goes wrong with my curtains?
faqs.a: Be aware that curtains, like carpets and leather, sit outside the compensation cap in our terms and conditions. We would rather say that plainly than bury it. It is the reason we inspect at the window, pinch-test anything that looks sun-weakened, photograph the panels before takedown, and decline work where we think the fabric will not survive the process. Turning a job down is cheaper for everyone than ruining a pair of drapes.

services.body:
## What a press actually does

Steam ironing is not a household iron pushed harder. A press works with three things at once — moisture, heat and pressure. Steam relaxes the fibre so the old crease lets go, the head applies even pressure across the whole panel to set the new shape, and the moisture is drawn back out so the garment leaves the table dry rather than damp.

The part most people miss is the last one: cloth sets its shape as it cools, not while it is hot. A shirt that goes straight from the press into a bag will arrive with fresh creases no matter how well it was pressed. Everything here is hung or laid flat and allowed to cool before it is packed.

## Heat is decided by the fibre, not by the item

Cotton and linen take high heat and direct contact. Polyester, nylon and most viscose blends do not. Put a hot head straight onto polyester and you get glazing — a permanent shine, usually on shoulders, lapels and the seat of trousers, that no amount of re-pressing will lift. Those pieces go through steam and a press cloth instead of bare metal. Silk is worked at low heat and kept away from wet steam, because a single droplet condensing on silk leaves a ring you can see across a room. Wool is steamed and brushed back up rather than crushed flat.

## Nazuk kapde, extra care

Delicate work fails before the fabric does. Plastic sequins melt, hot-fix stones lift off their adhesive, and zari darkens under direct heat. Embellished kurtas, sherwanis and lehengas are pressed from the reverse under a cover cloth, or finished on a form so nothing bears the weight of the press head. Rubber and plastisol prints on T-shirts are turned inside out first — a print that touches a hot plate sticks to it. Saree and skirt pleats are set by hand, not squashed.

## What a press genuinely cannot fix

Heat sets stains. Pressing is the fastest way to make a faint tea, sweat or deodorant mark permanent, so anything with a visible mark should be washed or dry cleaned first — if we spot one at sorting, we will call you before it goes on the table. Bubbling or rippling along a shirt collar or cuff is the interlining adhesive failing; heat makes that worse, not better, and it cannot be pressed out. Shine on the seat of well-worn wool trousers can be softened with steam and a brush but not reversed once the fibres are flattened. Fold lines that have sat under weight in viscose or rayon for months often will not drop fully. And linen will never come back looking like cotton — a soft crease is simply what the fibre does.

## Before you hand it over

Empty every pocket: pens, coins, blister packs, notes. Make sure nothing has been stored damp, because heat locks that musty smell in. Your mattress absorbs more than anything else in the house and gets cleaned the least. Every night you lose moisture and skin into its top few centimetres, and that thin layer is the whole problem. It is where dust mites live, because skin is what they eat, and what sets off the morning sneezing is not the mite but the protein in its droppings, which lifts out of the fibres every time you turn over.

In Gurugram it builds faster than people expect. Monsoon humidity keeps most flats comfortable enough for mites to breed, and the rest of the year the bedroom is shut, air-conditioned and barely ventilated. Airing it in the sun is not an option on the eleventh floor of a Sector 49 tower with a balcony the size of a side table.

## What the job actually involves

We work in your home. A mattress cannot go downstairs unfolded, and folding damages a spring unit or foam core, so it stays on the bed.

Dry work comes first: HEPA vacuuming with an agitating head across the whole surface, into the seams, along the piping and over both faces. That alone lifts skin, hair, grit and much of the mite matter before any liquid touches the fabric. Then targeted treatment. Sweat and body oil show as yellow-brown haloes around the head and hip areas, and those are pre-sprayed, given dwell time and extracted. Urine, from a child or a pet, needs an enzyme that breaks down uric acid crystals, because plain detergent only masks the smell and it returns the first humid week.

Everything is low-moisture, and that restraint is the craft. A soaked mattress can take days to dry from the inside and will grow mould in the foam long before it feels damp to the hand. We use controlled extraction with strong vacuum recovery and airflow, and we do not pack up until the surface is dry. Leave the bed unmade and a fan running.

## What cannot be saved

- **Old sweat yellowing.** The residue, odour and bacteria come out. The tint usually stays, because oxidised body oil has already changed the ticking's colour. Anyone promising a ten-year-old yellowed mattress will come back white is guessing.
- **Mould inside the foam.** Black speckling under the ticking means it has grown into the material, and no surface process reaches it.
- **Heat-set blood.** Blood only lifts cold. Once it has been washed hot or pressed over, it is fixed.
- **A collapsed core.** A permanent body-shaped dip means the core has failed. We can make it hygienic; we cannot make it supportive.
- **Coir and cotton-filled mattresses.** These hold water badly, so we treat them dry with surface steam only, and we tell you that before starting.

## Before we arrive

Strip the bedding and wash it at 60°C if the label allows, since a cooler wash moves mites around rather than killing them. Clear anything stored under the bed and give us access to one long side. Check for a zip-off cover, which can be laundered separately, and read the care label: a few imported mattresses are marked do not wet clean, and we go fully dry on those. Most of all, tell us what happened on it: a spill, an illness, a pet accident. It decides what we bring.

faqs.q: Do you take the mattress away or clean it at home?
faqs.a: At home, always. A mattress has to be folded to get it into a lift or down a stairwell, and folding is what damages a spring unit or a foam core. Our team comes to you with everything needed and works on the bed where it stands. Only removable items, such as a zip-off cover or a topper, may go back to our Sushant Lok or Sector 49 store for a proper wash.

faqs.q: How long before we can sleep on it again?
faqs.a: We do not leave until the surface is dry to the hand, and we run airflow over it before we pack up. How long the inside takes depends on the mattress: a pocket-spring unit breathes far faster than dense foam, and coir slowest of all. We will tell you on the day what to expect for yours. Keep the bed unmade and a fan on until then, and do not put a plastic sheet over it.

faqs.q: Will the yellow sweat stains actually go?
faqs.a: Honestly, usually not completely. Sweat and body oil oxidise over time and change the colour of the ticking itself, so what you are looking at is dyed fabric, not surface dirt. We remove the residue, the odour and the bacteria, and the marks lighten. If someone tells you an old yellowed mattress will come back white, be careful. We would rather set the expectation before we start than after.

faqs.q: Can you deal with bed bugs?
faqs.a: No, and we will say so plainly. We are cleaners, not a licensed pest control service. Cleaning removes dust, allergens and mite matter, but it will not eradicate a bed bug infestation, and doing a clean first only wastes your money. Get a proper pest treatment done, then call us afterwards to take out the residue and refresh the mattress.

faqs.q: Is it safe for a memory foam or latex mattress?
faqs.a: Yes, with the right method. Memory foam and latex are both sensitive to over-wetting and to harsh alkaline chemistry, so they get lower moisture, a milder solution and a longer drying stage than a spring mattress would. Latex in particular does not tolerate strong cleaners. Tell us the type when you book so we bring the correct chemistry rather than deciding at your door.

faqs.q: My child wet the bed months ago and the smell keeps returning in humid weather. Why?
faqs.a: Because ordinary detergent washes away the odour but leaves the uric acid crystals in the fibres. When humidity rises they reactivate and the smell comes back. That is a classic monsoon complaint in Gurugram. It needs an enzyme treatment with enough dwell time to break the crystals down, followed by extraction. If the urine soaked right through to the core years ago, be realistic: we may reduce it rather than end it.

faqs.q: How often is it worth doing?
faqs.a: For most Gurugram homes, once or twice a year is sensible, and it is worth timing one of those just after the monsoon. Bring it forward if anyone in the house has allergies or asthma, if there is a pet on the bed, or if the mattress has never been cleaned. Between visits, a washable mattress protector and washing bedding at 60°C does more good than anything else.

services.body:
## What wet cleaning actually is

Wet cleaning is professional cleaning in water. That sounds like what your machine at home does, and it isn't. The difference is control. A wet cleaning machine holds water temperature inside a narrow band, rotates the drum slowly with long pauses between reversals, and keeps both the water level and the extraction speed low. Detergents are pH-matched to the fibre: mildly alkaline for cotton and linen, near-neutral or slightly acidic for wool and silk. Wool felts and shrinks when alkalinity, heat and agitation arrive together. Take away any one of the three and the garment survives.

Then there is finishing, which is where most of the actual work sits. Wet-cleaned garments leave the machine damp on purpose, at roughly eighty to ninety per cent dry. Over-drying wool in a tumbler is what shrinks it, not the water. The rest of the moisture comes out on tensioning and steam finishing equipment that pulls the garment back to its cut shape while it dries. Skip that step and even a perfectly washed jacket comes back looking a size smaller.

## When water beats solvent

Dry cleaning solvent is excellent on oil: cooking grease, cosmetics, wax, engine marks. It is poor at everything water-soluble. Sweat, deodorant, salt, sugar, soft drinks, milk, tea, blood and urine are all water-based soils, and solvent simply leaves them in the cloth. In Gurugram that matters more than it would in a cooler city. From April to June, most of what is sitting in a shirt collar is pasina and body salts rather than oil, and that load only comes out in water.

Wet cleaning also leaves no solvent residue and no solvent smell, which is why we prefer it for baby clothes, bedding, gym wear and anything worn against skin all day.

## What we cannot save

Some damage arrives already done. Chlorine bleach spots on coloured cotton are not stains, they are missing dye, and nothing brings the colour back. Yellowed underarm staining that has been set by an iron over several years has usually degraded the fibre itself, and whitening it further weakens it to the point of opening a hole. Perspiration combined with antiperspirant on silk can strip dye permanently. Dried emulsion paint is permanent. Old sugar stains from juice, cola or white wine are invisible when fresh and caramelise into a brown mark months later, so tell us where you spilled something even if you cannot see anything there today.

Some garments are also not wet cleaning candidates at all. Fused jacket fronts and cheap bonded interlinings can bubble and delaminate in water. Real zari, mukaish and glued-on sequins do not tolerate it. Unfixed dyes on bandhani, hand-block prints and some deep-dyed silks bleed. We test for dye bleed on an inside seam before anything goes in, and if the test fails the item goes to solvent instead, or comes back to you untouched with an explanation.

## Before you hand the item over

Empty every pocket, pens especially. Point out each stain, say what caused it, and tell us if you already tried something at home. A mark that has had vinegar, bleach or a supermarket spray on it behaves very differently, and we need to know before we treat it. Flag loose buttons, seam splits and moth holes so they get recorded at pickup rather than discovered at delivery.

faqs.q: My label says dry clean only. Can you still wet clean it?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but never automatically. Care labels in India are usually written as the safest possible instruction rather than the only workable one, so a dry clean only tag frequently sits on a garment that water handles better. We decide by fibre, construction and a dye-bleed test on an inside seam, not by the label alone. If the test or the construction says no, we use solvent instead and tell you why.

faqs.q: Will my woollens shrink?
faqs.a: Shrinkage in wool comes from three things acting together: alkaline detergent, heat and mechanical agitation. Wet cleaning removes all three from the equation with fibre-matched pH, controlled temperature and a slow drum. The bigger risk is drying, which is why woollens come out of the machine still damp and are finished on tensioning equipment rather than tumbled dry.

faqs.q: How is this different from a normal wash at home?
faqs.a: Same medium, completely different control. At home you have one or two wash programmes, tap water at whatever hardness Gurugram gives you that day, a general-purpose detergent and a dryer that runs until the clothes are bone dry. Wet cleaning is programmed per garment type, uses conditioned water and fibre-specific chemistry, and treats drying as a shaping step rather than a heat step.

faqs.q: Is wet cleaning better than dry cleaning?
faqs.a: Neither one wins outright, and anyone who says otherwise is selling you something. Solvent is better on oil, grease, wax and cosmetics. Water is better on sweat, salt, deodorant, sugar, food and drink spills, and general body soil. Most wardrobes need both, which is why we grade every item on arrival instead of pushing everything through one process.

faqs.q: Does it get rid of the dry cleaner smell?
faqs.a: Yes, because there is no solvent involved at any stage, so there is nothing left in the fibre to smell. This is the main reason customers move baby clothes, bedding, innerwear and everyday office shirts over to wet cleaning.

faqs.q: Can you wet clean a suit?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on how the jacket is built. A canvassed or half-canvassed jacket, where the chest piece is stitched in, usually wet cleans well and comes back better than it would from solvent if the soiling is body-based. A fully fused jacket, where the interlining is glued, can bubble or separate in water. We check the construction before committing, and a trouser can often be wet cleaned even when its jacket cannot.

faqs.q: What about down jackets and puffers?
faqs.a: Down is one of the clearest cases for water. Solvent strips the natural oils out of the down clusters and the jacket loses loft permanently. Wet cleaning with the right detergent keeps the down alive, though it needs a long, low-heat drying and breaking cycle afterwards to restore the fill.

## A bag is not a garment

A shirt is one layer of cloth. A bag is a sandwich — outer material, a stiffener of card, foam or buckram, glue holding the two together, and a lining. Put it in a machine and water doesn't just clean, it softens the adhesive: panels bubble, the stiffener collapses, and the bag never sits upright again. Nothing here goes into a drum. Every bag is worked by hand, panel by panel, with as little moisture as the material allows.

We clean a whole panel rather than dabbing at one mark. Spot-cleaning a leather flap leaves a clean ring on a dirty panel, which looks worse than the stain did. Seam to seam is the only honest way.

## The inside is usually the worse half

Foundation, lipstick, sanitiser, crumbs, a leaked pen, coins that print grey rings into a cream lining. Lining is normally glued to the shell, so it can't be turned out and scrubbed — it is cleaned in place, damp, and dried slowly. The padded back of a laptop backpack is the same problem in foam: it holds water, and a bag that goes home not-quite-dry smells worse than when it arrived. Drying is measured in days, off heat and out of direct sun, stuffed so the bag holds its own shape. A Cyber City commute pushes more grit through one tote in a month than a wardrobe sees in a year: roz wahi dhool, the same dust daily.

## What we can't fix, and would rather say first

- **Worn corners and flaked edge paint.** Cleaning does not put leather back onto an abraded corner or re-lay lost edge coat. That is recolouring, a different job — and we'll say so.
- **PU or bonded "leather" that has begun to peel.** After a few years in NCR humidity the coating breaks down. Cleaning only speeds the flaking, so we show you and hand the bag back.
- **Ballpoint ink in a pale lining.** Ink is a dye and solvent moves it sideways. We can usually reduce it; a faint ghost normally stays.
- **Oil in suede or nubuck.** Once oil has sat in the nap it is structural, not surface.
- **Patina and rain spotting on untreated tan leather** — the pale handles and trim on some designer bags darken with use and don't go back.
- **Anything already attacked at home** with acetone, nail-polish remover, glass cleaner or baby wipes. The finish is often gone under the mark before we ever see it.

One more honest point: dirt hides wear. A properly clean bag sometimes shows its thin spots and old scuffs more clearly, because no grime is left to even them out.

## Before you hand it over

Empty every pocket — cards, earrings, coins, medicine strips, especially pens. Detach charms and any strap you're attached to. Point out cracked coating, loose stitching, a split lining or colour transfer from dark denim, and we note it on your receipt at the door, the same way we count a laundry order with you.

After the monsoon, if a bag came out of the cupboard smelling musty, don't store it back in plastic. Use a breathable cotton bag stuffed with clean paper, not newspaper — newsprint transfers onto light leather.

faqs.q: Can you just put my backpack in a washing machine? It says machine-washable on the label.
faqs.a: Some nylon daypacks genuinely survive it, but the foam back panel and shoulder straps hold water for days and that is where the smell comes from. We hand-clean, rinse in a controlled way and then dry the padding through properly. On technical packs, a machine wash with ordinary detergent also strips the water-repellent finish on the outer fabric, which you don't get back.

faqs.q: The corners of my handbag are worn down to the base material. Will cleaning fix that?
faqs.a: No. Cleaning removes soil; it cannot replace leather that has abraded away or edge paint that has flaked off a strap. That work is recolouring and refinishing, a different job with a different result. We'll tell you honestly at intake whether cleaning alone will make a visible difference on your bag.

faqs.q: A pen burst inside my bag. Is the lining recoverable?
faqs.a: Usually only partly. Ballpoint ink is a dye, and the solvents that lift it also carry it sideways into clean fabric, so aggressive work can make the patch bigger. We reduce it as far as the lining safely allows and normally leave a faint ghost. If the lining is pale nylon, expect improvement rather than removal.

faqs.q: My bag has been in the cupboard since the monsoon and smells musty, with white specks on the leather.
faqs.a: Bring it in sooner rather than later. Surface mildew on finished leather generally cleans off well and the smell goes with it. What we can't undo is pitting where the fungus has eaten into the finish. And if it goes back into the same plastic cover in the same cupboard, it will return — store it in breathable cotton with a little air around it.

faqs.q: Do you clean designer bags?
faqs.a: Yes, and we'd rather see those in person first at Sector 43 or Sector 49 so we can look at the construction, the hardware and any untreated tan leather trim before quoting on what's achievable. Vintage pieces and exotic skins are always an in-store assessment, never a blind pickup.

faqs.q: I already tried cleaning it at home. Does that change anything?
faqs.a: It can. Baby wipes, glass cleaner and nail-polish remover strip or darken the surface finish, and the damage often sits under the mark you were trying to remove. Tell us what you used — it changes what we can attempt and stops us making it worse.

faqs.q: Can you clean the inside of a trolley case after something leaked in it?
faqs.a: Usually yes. The interior lining and the compression panels are cleaned and dried out fully, which is the part that matters for smell. We don't dismantle telescopic handles or wheel housings, so grit trapped deep inside those channels stays; scuff marks transferred onto a hard shell by other cases at the airport normally come off, but gouges in the shell are structural.

services.body:
## Leather is a skin, not a fabric

Every hide that becomes a jacket or a bag is packed with fats during tanning. Those fats sit between the fibres and let them slide past each other, which is the whole reason good leather drapes instead of behaving like cardboard. Any cleaning that lifts soil also takes some of that fat with it. So cleaning and reconditioning are one job here, not two: leather cleaned and handed straight back, unfed, will stiffen within a season. It is also why leather never goes through water immersion the way a shirt does.

## The finish decides everything

Before anything touches your item, we work out what the surface actually is. A drop of water on pigmented leather beads and sits; on aniline it darkens and sinks within seconds. Pigmented leather, which covers most jackets and most branded handbags, carries a thin coloured topcoat and takes a proper surface clean well. Aniline and semi-aniline are dyed through with little or no topcoat, so they absorb whatever touches them and usually have to be worked panel by panel rather than spot by spot, because evening out the whole panel is the only way to avoid leaving a halo around the mark. Suede and nubuck have no topcoat at all and are brushed, blocked and re-napped dry, never shampooed. Guessing wrong at this first step is what ruins leather, and it is usually where a home attempt has already gone wrong before the item reaches us.

## What cannot be saved, and we say so first

- **Ballpoint ink on unfinished leather.** The ink dye has already travelled into the fibre. Anything strong enough to lift it lifts the leather's own colour with it.
- **Sun fading.** That is lost dye, not dirt, so cleaning does nothing for it. Recolouring is a separate job and it changes how the leather feels in the hand.
- **Splits in the grain.** Conditioning softens the leather around a crack and makes it much less obvious. The crack itself does not close.
- **Bonded or PU "leather" that has begun peeling.** Nothing puts a delaminated coating back down.
- **Old oil, ghee and food grease.** Months-old fat has bonded with the leather's own oils. We can usually reduce it to a faint shadow, and you should be sceptical of anyone promising more.
- **Deep monsoon mould.** Surface growth comes off. Where it has pitted the grain, the pitting stays and sometimes the smell does too.

## Before you hand it over

Empty every pocket, twice. A forgotten pen inside a jacket sleeve or bag lining is the most common way a good leather piece is lost for good. Tell us what the stain is and, honestly, what you already tried at home, because coconut oil, baby wipes and shoe polish all change what we are able to do next. Detach fur trims, remove keyrings and charms, and point out existing cracks or scuffs while we count the order with you at your door, so we are both looking at the same item from the start.

faqs.q: Can a leather jacket go through normal dry cleaning?
faqs.a: No. A standard dry cleaning cycle is built for woven fabric, and the tumbling and solvent exposure strip the fats out of a hide far faster than they lift the soil. Leather is worked by hand, surface by surface, and then reconditioned. If a leather jacket has a fabric lining, the lining is treated as its own job, because sweat salts around the collar and underarms need a different approach from the outer skin.

faqs.q: My light-coloured bag has denim colour rubbed onto one side. Will it come off?
faqs.a: Often, on smooth pigmented leather, because the indigo has transferred onto the topcoat rather than into the hide. On light suede or nubuck it is much harder, since the dye sits down in the nap with nothing sealing the surface. We will look at the panel and tell you honestly whether we expect a full lift or only a reduction before we start.

faqs.q: Will cleaning change the colour of my leather?
faqs.a: Conditioning usually deepens the tone very slightly, which most people read as the item looking richer. The real risk is patchiness, and that comes from spot-treating an aniline or suede item. We avoid it by working the whole panel rather than just the mark. If your item is already faded in places, cleaning will make that unevenness easier to see, not less, and we will point that out at the door rather than after.

faqs.q: My leather jacket has been shut in the wardrobe since last winter and smells damp. Can that be fixed?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Gurugram's monsoon humidity in a closed wardrobe is the single most common reason leather comes to us in September and October. Surface mould and the musty smell that goes with it can be cleaned off and the leather refed. Where the growth has been sitting long enough to pit the grain, the pitting is permanent and a trace of odour can remain, so bring it in as soon as you notice it rather than waiting for the cold.

faqs.q: What happens to zips, buckles and chains?
faqs.a: Metal is cleaned and masked off so conditioner does not sit on it, and hardware is polished where polishing helps. What we cannot do is put plating back. Once brass or gold-tone plating has worn through on a handle ring or a buckle edge, that is a re-plating job with a metal workshop, not a cleaning one. We will show you where the wear is instead of quietly working around it.

faqs.q: How do you dry leather?
faqs.a: Slowly, at room temperature, away from sunlight, heaters and fans blowing hot air. Bags are stuffed and shaped so the panels do not collapse while they lose moisture, and shoes are treed or packed for the same reason. Fast heat drying is exactly what shrinks a hide and makes it hard, and it is why a jacket dried on a balcony after rain never feels the same again.

faqs.q: Do you collect from home?
faqs.a: Yes. Free pickup and delivery across Gurugram, or drop the item at our Sector 43 store on Vyapar Kendra Road or the Sector 49 store at Unitech Arcadia. Every item is counted with you at the door, your order is packed separately from every other customer's, and you get a written receipt of what was collected. For leather that matters, because a one-off jacket or bag is not something you want going into a shared pile.

services.body:
## The dirt you can see is not the problem

A soft toy is three things stacked together: an outer pile fabric, a stuffing core, and often some hardware buried in the middle. Nearly all the trouble lives in that middle layer. Surface dust brushes off a teddy in seconds. What actually makes a toy smell is dried saliva, spilt milk, sweat and fine Gurugram road dust that has worked its way down into the fibrefill. That is why wiping a toy down or spraying it fresh lasts about two days: the source is untouched, sitting an inch deep. Ground-floor flats around Sushant Lok and Sector 49 see it faster than most, because toys on open shelves are very good dust traps and one damp monsoon is enough to give a well-loved bear that closed-cupboard smell.

## How we choose the method

Before anything gets wet, we work out what is inside. We feel along the seams for a squeaker, a music box, a battery pouch or wire in the limbs, and we identify the filling. Polyester fibrefill takes a full wet clean comfortably. Foam chips and plastic pellets hold water, gain a lot of weight and can pull the outer fabric permanently out of shape, so those are surface-cleaned, or wet-cleaned with a much longer and gentler dry. Electronics come out through an opened seam and go back in with the seam restitched. If a unit is sealed in and cannot be reached, we clean without immersion and tell you that upfront. We then test colourfastness on a hidden seam, since red felt tongues, printed cheeks and dyed ribbon are the usual bleeders onto cream plush.

## Drying is most of the job

Cleaning a soft toy is straightforward. Drying one properly is not. A toy can feel dry on the outside while the core is still wet, and a damp core turns sour within a week and can grow mould at the centre that never comes out. We dry long, at low heat, with movement, so the fill redistributes instead of setting into hard lumps. Lumpy stuffing is the classic result of a hot home machine wash, and once it sets it does not come back. Because these toys get chewed, rinsing matters as much as washing: we run extra rinses so nothing is left sitting in the pile, and we do not use harsh chlorine bleach on anything meant for a child.

## What we cannot save

Sun-faded plush cannot be re-dyed. Pile that has matted from years of hugging comes back clean but not fluffy, and brushing helps only so far. Ballpoint ink and permanent marker on plush do not come out. Milk, blood or vomit that has already been hot-washed at home is usually set for good. Glued-on eyes and noses sometimes let go during cleaning, and a glued feature is always more of a risk than a stitched or locked one. Perished foam in older toys, the orange crumbly kind, disintegrates the moment it gets wet. If an item falls into any of these, we say so before we start, not after.

## Before you hand it over

Photograph the toy from both sides. Take off clothing and accessories and keep them at home. Point out loose seams and old repairs, because a weak seam opens under proper cleaning and we would rather stitch it first. Mention batteries. Above all, tell us if this is the toy that has to be there at bedtime, jiske bina neend nahi aati, so we can flag it as irreplaceable. Many parents send it while the child is away for a few days, or send the second-favourite first to see how it comes back. Every order is counted with you at the door, packed separately from every other customer's order, and acknowledged with a written receipt at pickup.

The metre-tall bears that no home machine will take. These need the longest drying of anything we handle, because the core sits so far from the surface.
Pellets and foam chips hold water and can stretch the outer fabric out of shape. We either surface-clean these or wet-clean with a much slower dry, and we tell you which before starting.
Where the unit can be reached, we open a seam, take it out, clean the toy and restitch. Where it is sealed in, the toy is cleaned without immersion.

faqs.q: My son's teddy has a music box inside. Can it still be cleaned?
faqs.a: Usually yes. If the unit is reachable, we open a seam, remove it, clean the toy fully and restitch. If it is sealed inside a moulded pocket we cannot reach, we clean the toy without immersion instead. That gets the surface and a fair bit of the smell, but not the whole core, and we will tell you that before you leave it with us rather than after.

faqs.q: The toy is about eight years old and the fur has gone flat and rough. Will it look new again?
faqs.a: No, and anyone who says otherwise is guessing. Matted pile is fibre that has been physically crushed and felted by years of hugging and washing. Cleaning removes the grime, and brushing lifts the pile as far as it will go, but the softness of new plush does not return. What you will get is a genuinely clean, fresh-smelling toy with the same texture.

We also keep harsh chlorine bleach away from children's items entirely, which is why heavily yellowed white plush stays slightly off-white with us.

Send it as it is, tell us what happened and roughly when, and let us treat it. Do not try to sanitise it with hot water first.

faqs.q: Do you take giant soft toys?
faqs.a: Yes, and they are one of the main reasons people call us for this, since nothing that size fits a domestic machine. The thing to know is that a large toy takes considerably longer than a small one, almost entirely because of drying. Rushing a big toy out half-dry is how it develops mould at the centre, so we do not do it.

## The fill decides the method, not the cover

The outer fabric of a quilt tells you very little. What matters is the fill, and that is the first thing checked when a razai or duvet is opened out flat.

Loose cotton batting, the filling in most hand-stitched razais, behaves badly in water: it swells, shifts and sets into hard ridges as it dries, so the razai comes back thin down the middle and heavy at one end. Those are cleaned with solvent and kept flat throughout. Down and feather duvets are the opposite case, because solvent strips the oil out of down and leaves it brittle, so they are washed gently instead. Polyester and microfibre comforters take water well, provided the quilting stitch is still holding the fill in place.

## Drying is the actual job

Washing a quilt is the easy half. Drying one right through to the core is where it goes wrong at home. A duvet that is ninety-five per cent dry feels dry in your hands, then smells of damp cupboard within a week, and mildew starting in that trapped moisture will spot the shell permanently. So drying is long, low-heat and interrupted: the item comes out partway, the fill is broken up and redistributed by hand, and it goes back in. That is also what brings loft back to a duvet and lifts the nap on a mink or plush blanket.

## What cannot be saved

Honest answers are more useful than optimistic ones.

- Body-oil yellowing on a white duvet shell, oxidised over seasons in storage. It lightens. It rarely disappears.
- Black mildew spotting where the fungus has eaten into the fibre. That pigment sits inside the damaged fibre, not on top of it.
- Down that has already been through a hot home wash and clumped. The quills fracture and the loft does not come back.
- Scorch or melt marks on polyester fill, from an iron or a room heater standing too close.
- Dye bleed that has already run, usually after a dark razai cover was soaked in a bucket at home.

If a stain is not going to shift, you will be told while the item is being counted at your door, not afterwards.

## Before you hand it over

Take the cover off and look at the quilt itself, because a folded quilt hides stains beautifully. Run a hand along the seams for splits: agitation turns a small split into a fill explosion, so point it out and it gets stitched shut first. Pull out any safety pins holding a cover in place. And say if something has already been tried at home, bleach or Dettol or a stain spray, because it changes what is chemically possible afterwards.

## Timing and storage

The sensible time to get razais done is at the end of winter, before they go into storage, not on the first cold night in November when all of Gurugram wants theirs back at once. Sardi se pehle, razai ready. Store them in a cotton bag or an old bedsheet, never a sealed plastic packet, and keep naphthalene balls in a cloth pouch rather than against the fabric, where they leave marks.

Bedding is bulky to carry to a shop, so pickup and delivery is free across Gurugram. Every piece is counted with you at the door, packed separately, and acknowledged with a written receipt.

faqs.q: Can my razai be washed, or does it have to be dry cleaned?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the filling. A hand-stitched razai filled with loose cotton batting should not be put through water — the cotton swells, migrates to one end and dries into hard ridges, and no amount of shaking afterwards redistributes it evenly. Those are solvent-cleaned and handled flat. A polyester-filled comforter or a down duvet is a different item altogether and is washed. We decide after opening it out, not from the label.

faqs.q: Will the filling go lumpy or bunch up at one end?
faqs.a: That is exactly what the method choice and the drying stage are there to prevent. The item is dried in long, low-heat stages and taken out partway so the fill can be broken up and redistributed by hand before it sets. The one case where lumping is not reversible is down that has previously been through a hot home wash — once the quills have fractured and matted, the loft is gone permanently and nothing brings it back.

faqs.q: My white duvet has yellow patches. Will they come out?
faqs.a: Usually they lighten rather than disappear. Yellowing on a duvet shell is body oil that has soaked in and oxidised, often over several winters in storage, and by the time it is visible through the cover it has been there a long time. We will treat it and tell you honestly what improvement is realistic before starting, rather than after.

faqs.q: It has been in storage all summer and smells of mothballs and damp. Can that be removed?
faqs.a: Naphthalene and camphor smell almost always goes, because it responds to cleaning plus proper airing rather than to perfume sprayed over it. Musty storage smell usually goes too. The caution is that if damp storage has already left black mildew spots on the fabric, the smell can leave while the spots stay, because the fungus has stained the fibre from inside.

faqs.q: Should I send the cover along with the quilt?
faqs.a: Yes, send both. They are washed as a set so the colour and finish stay matched, and it also lets us check whether a dark cover has been bleeding dye into the filling, which is common with cheaply dyed razai covers. Take the cover off before we collect so you can spot any stains hidden in the folds, and remove any safety pins.

faqs.q: Do you clean electric blankets or weighted blankets?
faqs.a: Electric blankets and anything with wiring or heating elements sewn inside are not accepted — cleaning risks damaging the element, and a damaged element is a shock and fire risk you would only discover later. For weighted blankets and unusual fills, send us a photo of the care label on WhatsApp first and we will tell you straight away whether it is something we can take.

faqs.a: Pickup and delivery is free across Gurugram, which matters most for bedding because razais and duvets are awkward to carry to a shop. Call or WhatsApp +91 63 67 600 500 to book, or drop items at either store: Vyapar Kendra in Sushant Lok Phase I, Sector 43, or Unitech Arcadia in Sector 49.
