## What linen actually gets dirty with

Most bedsheets are not dirty the way a shirt is dirty. The soil is body oil: sebum, hair oil, night cream, dried sweat, spread thinly across the whole sheet and concentrated in a band along the top hem and on the pillowcases. It stays invisible for months, then one day the pillowcase looks yellow-grey and no amount of detergent shifts it. Oil does not come out with detergent alone at the temperature a domestic machine runs. It needs an alkaline pre-soak and an enzyme stage with real contact time before the wash even begins. That is the step a home wash skips, and it is where we start.

The second problem is local. Water across most of Gurugram is hard, and calcium binds to both the cotton and the soap, leaving a mineral film in towel loops and inside the weave of sheets. That film is what makes towels stiff, scratchy and slow to absorb. It is not age. An acidic descaling rinse takes it out, while adding more detergent makes it worse. If your towels have gone crunchy despite regular washing, this is almost always the reason.

## What can and cannot be saved

Hair oil, sebum yellowing, sweat, tea, coffee and cooking grease on table linen usually come out, often completely. Haldi on white cotton normally reduces to nothing, but on polyester or poly-cotton the turmeric bonds to the fibre and can leave a faint yellow shadow, so we tell you which fabric you have before promising anything.

Some things genuinely cannot be recovered. Benzoyl peroxide from acne creams and face washes, hair colour, and bleach splashes are not stains at all. They have stripped the dye out of the fabric, and nothing puts colour back. Mildew from linen packed away slightly damp through the monsoon can often be lightened, but mildew feeds on cotton, so where it has been sitting a while the fibre is already weak and small holes may open during washing. We point that out before we wash. Rust from a leaking iron or a rusty drying rack needs an acidic reducer and never chlorine, and it does not always clear fully.

## Before you hand it over

Check hems and corners for small tears, because agitation turns a two-inch split into a six-inch one. Empty duvet covers; socks and phone chargers arrive inside them more often than you would expect. Tell us what you have already tried at home, and whether the piece has been ironed since the stain happened, because heat sets oil and protein into the fibre and changes what is still possible. Mention any new or dark set that has not been washed before, since indigo and maroon prints bleed on the first few washes and we will run those on their own.

One last thing worth knowing: a double bedsheet in a domestic machine has nowhere to tumble, so most of the load gets almost no mechanical action. That is the quiet reason home-washed sheets stay dull however good the detergent is.

faqs.q: My white pillowcases have gone yellow even though I wash them every week. Can that be reversed?
faqs.a: Usually yes. That yellowing is oxidised body oil and hair oil that a normal wash never lifted, so it built up layer by layer. It responds to an alkaline pre-soak plus enzyme treatment with proper contact time, which is what a domestic cycle cannot give it. The exception is a pillowcase that has been ironed many times over the same soiling, because heat drives oil deeper into the fibre. Those come back much lighter but not always perfectly white, and we will say so when we see them.

faqs.q: Will my towels actually come back soft?
faqs.a: Softer, and more absorbent, but through a different route than you might expect. We do not use fabric softener on towels because it coats the loops and is the main reason towels stop soaking up water. Instead we use an acidic descaling rinse that strips out the hard-water mineral film Gurugram supply leaves behind, which is what makes towels feel like cardboard. Honest limit: a towel whose pile has genuinely worn flat over years will feel clean and absorbent again, but it will not be new.

faqs.q: There is a haldi mark on my tablecloth. Is it coming out?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the fibre, not on how old the mark is. On white or light cotton, turmeric almost always reduces to nothing. On polyester or a poly-cotton blend it bonds to the fibre and a faint yellow shadow often stays permanently. We check the composition first and tell you which situation you are in before we treat it, so you are not paying in hope.

faqs.q: Do my sheets get washed with other people's laundry?
faqs.a: No. Every order is bagged on its own and stays separate from every other customer's order through the whole process. Your bedsheets, pillowcases and towels are counted with you at the door before they leave, and you get a written receipt of exactly what was collected. When the order comes back, count it again against that receipt.

faqs.q: I have a brand new dark bedsheet set. Should I wash it once at home before sending it?
faqs.a: Please do not. Send it as it is and tell us it is new. Deep indigo, maroon and traditional block prints release loose dye for the first few washes, and a home wash is where that dye usually transfers onto something else in the load. We run new and unwashed dark sets on their own and test for bleed before committing the full cycle.

faqs.q: Can you clean the quilt or duvet itself, not just the cover?
faqs.a: The cover comes under linen cleaning. The filled quilt, duvet, comforter or blanket is handled by our blanket and quilt cleaning service, which uses a different process for bulk and drying. Send both together and we will route them correctly; they will still be counted and returned as one order.

faqs.a: Free pickup and delivery covers Gurugram. Call or WhatsApp +91 63 67 600 500, or email care@wash4you.in, and tell us roughly how many sheets, pillowcases, towels and table pieces you have so the collection is counted quickly at the door. services.body:
## What actually happens to a tie

A necktie is not one piece of fabric. It is an outer shell, a wool or cotton interlining that gives the knot its body, a tipping fabric at both ends, and a single slip stitch running the length of the back that lets the whole thing stretch and recover every time you tie it. Put that in water and the layers shrink at different rates. The shell ripples, the interlining twists, and nothing brings it back. So ties go through solvent cleaning, spotted by hand first, then finished over a shaped form so the edges stay softly rolled. A tie that comes back with hard, knife-flat edges has been ironed, not finished.

## Caps: check the brim before you hand it over

Press the peak of your cap between finger and thumb. If it feels papery and holds a crease, the stiffener inside is cardboard, and that cap can never be wet washed — the brim buckles and stays buckled. Plastic-stiffened peaks spring back and will take a controlled hand clean. The other thing we look at is the sweatband. That grey-white tide line is two problems in one: salt, which dissolves in water, and sebum, which does not, so a cap needs both an aqueous and a solvent step to shift it. Sweat that has sat through a Gurugram summer oxidises into the cotton and yellows it. We can usually lighten that. We cannot always erase it, and we will tell you which one you are getting before we start.

## Scarves, stoles and dupattas

Pashmina, cashmere and fine wool are washed by hand with no agitation and dried flat, because a wet knit stretches under its own weight the moment you hang it. Fringes are combed straight while still damp; left alone they dry into knots that then have to be worked loose dry, which sheds fibre. Block-printed and bandhani dupattas get tested hardest, since a lot of hand-printed dye is unfixed, and one bleed test on a seam allowance is what stands between a beautiful dupatta and a pink haze across the white ground. Real zari is metal wrapped around a thread core: it tarnishes and it hates heat, so anything with zari, gota or sequins is pressed on the reverse, through a cloth, at low temperature.

## What cannot be saved

Turmeric on silk usually leaves a yellow ghost — curcumin is a dye, and it bonds to protein fibre. Perfume or attar sprayed straight onto a silk tie or scarf strips colour where it landed, and that pale patch is permanent. So is the faded line along the fold of a scarf that has hung in one position in a wardrobe for years; that is sunlight, not soil. Ink and paan are judged item by item. And if a tie has thinned at the knot after years of the same four-in-hand, cleaning will make that visible. It did not cause it.

## Before you hand the item over

Tell us what the stain is and roughly how old it is — that one sentence changes the chemistry we start with. Tell us if you have already tried something at home, because lemon, vinegar, toothpaste and hairspray all leave residues we have to work around. Take off brooches, tie pins and cap badges. Nazuk kapde, extra care — delicate things, handled slowly, and counted with you at the door before they leave.

faqs.q: Can you clean my baseball cap without wrecking the shape?
faqs.a: Usually, but it depends on the peak. Press it between your finger and thumb: if it feels like stiff card and holds a crease, the stiffener is cardboard and water will buckle it permanently, so we will hand-clean only the crown and sweatband and leave the brim dry. If the peak springs back, it is plastic and the whole cap can take a controlled hand clean and be dried on a former so the crown keeps its shape.

faqs.q: I spilt something on my silk tie and dabbed it with water. Have I made it worse?
faqs.a: Possibly, and it is the most common thing customers do. Water on silk moves the sizing outward and dries into a ring, so you can end up with a watermark that is larger than the original stain. Stop there. Do not rub, do not use soap, do not hold it under a tap. Let it dry, bring it in as it is, and tell us what the spill was.

faqs.q: Will you clean a heavy dupatta with zari and sequins on it?
faqs.a: Yes. Zari is real metal wound on a thread core, so it tarnishes with harsh chemistry and distorts with heat. We clean around it, press on the reverse through a cloth at low temperature, and never put a hot iron directly on the work. If sequins are glued rather than stitched, we will point that out before starting, because glue can soften.

faqs.q: Can accessories come along with my regular laundry pickup?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the easiest way to send them. Just tell the person at the door which items are accessories so they are logged and bagged separately rather than counted in with your shirts. They follow their own process and are packed on their own for return.

faqs.q: My scarf has an old stain and I have no idea what it was. Is it still worth sending?
faqs.a: Send it. Unknown stains are normal on accessories and we will still test and work it. What we will not do is promise a result we cannot see yet. After inspection we will tell you honestly whether we expect full removal, a visible improvement, or very little, and you decide from there.

faqs.q: Do you clean leather belts, gloves and watch straps here?
faqs.a: Those go to our leather care rather than accessories cleaning, because leather needs pH-balanced cleaning and conditioning instead of fabric chemistry. Send them anyway and we will route them correctly. Fabric belts, sashes and knitted gloves stay with accessories.

faqs.q: How should I store a tie or scarf between wears?
faqs.a: Roll a tie loosely and lay it in a drawer rather than hanging it folded over a rail, which sets a crease and stresses the bias. Store silk scarves flat or loosely rolled, and refold them along a different line now and then, since a scarf left in one fold for years fades along that line and no cleaning brings the colour back. We return ties rolled for exactly this reason.
